Adampol – Polonezköy

  • Adampol (Polonezköy) village centre

    Beykoz · 1842–

    A Polish village above the Bosphorus, founded in 1842 at Prince Adam Czartoryski's wish for countrymen without a country – and still alive more than 180 years on.

  • Founders' memorial, 150th anniversary (Czartoryski and Czajkowski)

    Beykoz · 1842 / 1992

    'A Polish village on Turkish soil' – so says the stone that 'grateful Adampol residents and compatriots from Poland' raised to the village's founders on its 150th anniversary.

  • Church of Our Lady of Częstochowa

    Beykoz · 1846 / 1914

    The church this Polish village waited almost twenty years for, built in 1914 with money collected in Poland – where in 1941 the future Pope John XXIII confirmed the village children.

  • Polish Catholic Cemetery, Polonezköy

    Beykoz · 1853–

    A cemetery the settlers cleared with their own hands – the resting place of insurgents, Crimean War veterans and generations of villagers.

  • Grave of Ludwika Śniadecka

    Beykoz · 1866

    The young Słowacki's first love and Sadyk Pasha's companion rests at Adampol – 'on Polish soil', as her epitaph says.

  • Zofia Ryży Memorial House ('Aunt Zosia's House')

    Beykoz · 1881–1883 / 1940

    To the whole village she was 'Aunt Zosia' – and, Poland's ambassador said, it was thanks to her that Polish did not die out in Adampol.

  • Adam Mickiewicz memorial plaque (1933)

    Beykoz · 1933

    'To our Bard' – in 1933 a Polish village near Istanbul honoured Mickiewicz with a plaque in two languages, calling him in Turkish 'our great poet'.

  • Memorial of Atatürk's 1937 visit

    Beykoz · 1937

    Village musicians played a krakowiak for Atatürk – and legend has it that the President then joined the dance.

  • Polonezköy Nature Park

    Beykoz · 1842 / 1994

    Walk the same forest the first settlers of Adampol entered more than 180 years ago – today some 3,000 protected hectares of oak, chestnut and beech.

The Great Emigration & Mickiewicz

  • Adam Mickiewicz Museum

    Beyoğlu · 1855 / 1955 / 1984

    On this spot Adam Mickiewicz died on 26 November 1855 – in the crypt of the house museum you will find a marble slab, a cross and a copy of the poet's death mask.

  • Grave of General Marian Langiewicz, Haidar Pasha Cemetery

    Üsküdar · 1866–1887

    For a few days in March 1863 he was dictator of the uprising – and he spent his last two decades in Istanbul as a modest railway clerk known as 'Langie Bey'.

  • Saint-Benoît – the Lazarists and the birth of Adampol

    Beyoğlu · 1842

    The Polish exiles received the land for Adampol in 1842 from the Lazarist fathers of this church – the story of the Polish village on the Bosphorus begins here.

  • Grave of Tadeusz Gasztowtt (Seyfeddin), Feriköy

    Şişli · 1909 / 1936

    A Paris-born Pole who became the Young Turk 'Seyfeddin' and in 1909 persuaded the Turks to honour Mickiewicz – he rests in the Feriköy cemetery.

Poles in the Sultan's Service

  • Cihangir – Sadyk Pasha and Ludwika Śniadecka

    Beyoğlu · 1861–1876

    In these lanes lived a Polish novelist who became a pasha; here the first love of the poet Słowacki died, and the Sultan's Polish court painter had his studio.

  • National Palaces Painting Museum – Chlebowski's paintings

    Beşiktaş · 1864–1876

    For twelve years a Polish painter worked for Sultan Abdülaziz – often from the Sultan's own sketches – and his portraits of the ruler belong to this museum.

  • Military Museum – Chlebowski's Battle of Varna

    Şişli · 1865–1872

    A Polish painter painted for the Sultan the Battle of Varna, where King Władysław III of Poland fell – the four-metre canvas belongs to this museum.

  • The Enderun Court: Wojciech Bobowski (Ali Ufkî)

    Fatih · ~1630–1675

    Wojciech Bobowski, a Pole known at the sultans' court as Ali Ufkî: he was said to know seventeen languages, and in 2005 The King's Singers recorded some of his psalms.

Envoys & Diplomacy

  • Site of the Elçi Han (Ambassadors' Inn)

    Fatih · 1622–1678

    Opposite the Column of Constantine most likely stood the inn that lodged the Commonwealth's great embassies: Prince Krzysztof Zbaraski in 1622 and, in 1677, Jan Gniński with a suite of 450.

  • The Sublime Porte (Bâbıâli)

    Fatih · 1677–1678

    ‘The envoy of Lechistan has not yet arrived’ – the hero of the best-loved Polish–Turkish legend is the grand vizier, and the gate of his office stands right here.

  • Topkapı Palace: Imperial Council Hall and Chamber of Petitions

    Fatih · 1622–1678

    This is how a Polish envoy's day with the sultan unfolded: pay for thousands of Janissaries, a banquet with the grand vizier, robes of honour – and only then the throne.

  • The former Polish Street (Leh Sokağı), today Nur-i Ziya Sokağı

    Beyoğlu · 1788–1793 / 1877–1878

    A side street off İstiklal long known as Leh Sokağı, 'Polish Street' – its name kept alive the 19th-century belief that Poland's embassy in Istanbul had never closed.

Wars & Captivity

  • Merzifonlu Kara Mustafa Pasha Complex

    Fatih · 1677–1691

    Poles knew Kara Mustafa long before Vienna: the envoy Jan Gniński spent months arguing with him over lands the sultan would not give back.

  • Area of the old slave market (Esir Pazarı)

    Fatih · 1500s–1847

    A place to remember the thousands taken captive from the lands of the Commonwealth – and the envoys and families who spent years raising ransoms to bring them home.

  • Imperial Gate of Topkapı Palace (Bâb-ı Hümâyûn)

    Fatih · 1620

    Polish embassies rode through this gate into the sultans' palace – and tradition links it with the memory of Hetman Żółkiewski, who fell at Cecora.

  • Yedikule Fortress (Castle of the Seven Towers)

    Fatih · 1620–1623

    Almost every Polish noble family had a relative who had suffered in “Jedykuła”, wrote Zygmunt Gloger of this fortress.

  • Tomb of Sultan Ahmed I (resting place of Osman II)

    Fatih · 1621–1622

    Here lies Sultan Osman II, who in 1621 faced Hetman Chodkiewicz at Khotyn – and who lost his throne and his life a few months after returning from that campaign.

Roxelana

  • Tomb of Hürrem Sultan (Roxelana)

    Fatih · ~1505–1558

    Here lies Roxelana, wife of Süleyman the Magnificent, whom Polish tradition places in Rohatyn – her letters to King Sigismund Augustus are still kept in a Warsaw archive.

  • Hürrem Sultan Hamam (Roxelana's Bath)

    Fatih · 1556

    The bathhouse Sinan himself built for Roxelana – by tradition a girl from Rohatyn – stands on the grandest spot in Istanbul, between Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque.

  • Haseki Hürrem Sultan Complex (Avratpazarı)

    Fatih · 1538–1551

    Roxelana's first great foundation: the mosque, madrasa, soup kitchen and hospital that the former captive from Ruthenia built here as the sultan's wife.

Churches, Cemeteries & John Paul II

  • St Anthony of Padua Basilica

    Beyoğlu · 1906–1912

    A Polish Franciscan from this basilica is pastor to the Poles of Turkey and also looks after the parish at Adampol – and for ten years the future Pope John XXIII preached here.

  • St Mary Draperis

    Beyoğlu · 1909

    In 1909 Turks and Poles prayed here together for the Polish volunteers who fell in the Crimean War – even the future last caliph came to the Mass.

  • Cathedral of the Holy Spirit (Saint-Esprit)

    Şişli · 1979

    Here on 29 November 1979 John Paul II said Mass for Istanbul's Catholics – and the next day, greeting his compatriots, he recalled the legend of the envoy of Lechistan: this time he had arrived at last.

  • Feriköy Latin Catholic Cemetery – memorial to Consul Wojciech Rychlewicz

    Şişli · 1937–1941 / 2021

    In 2021 Turkey's Chief Rabbi prayed in this Catholic cemetery, at the memorial to a Polish consul whose story had come to light only a year before.

  • Ecumenical Patriarchate, Phanar – John Paul II, 1979

    Fatih · 1979

    On St Andrew's day 1979 the Polish pope stood here beside the Patriarch of Constantinople and spoke of the wound of division that 'is not yet healed'.

  • Armenian Patriarchate, Kumkapı – John Paul II, 1979

    Fatih · 1979

    The least-known stop on the papal trail: on 29 November 1979 John Paul II came here to visit the Armenian Patriarch of Istanbul.

1939–1945

  • Kabataş – where the gold tanker Eocene anchored

    Beyoğlu · 1939

    While the ship lay at anchor here, diplomats argued over whether Poland's gold should go into the Ottoman Bank or on through the Dardanelles – with Germany pressing Turkey hard.

  • Haydarpaşa Station – where Poland's gold boarded the train

    Kadıköy · 1939

    By the time the German naval attaché reported to Berlin, Poland's gold had already been moved here from a British ship to a train bound for Syria.

Polish Istanbul Today

  • Consulate General of Poland in Istanbul

    Sarıyer (Maslak) · 1414–

    From Jagiełło's first envoys in 1414 to the secret wartime base 'Bey' of 1940–41: more than six centuries of Polish diplomacy on the Bosphorus now have an address in Maslak.
